title: Build the AI GTM Agent That Knows the Buyer - Dr. Sajjan Kanukolanu, Position2 (Position Squared)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is a multi-agent GTM system with ICP filter, match, and action agents structured across a three-layer architecture with a context graph, routing logic, and policy engine. The system serves B2B go-to-market operations, an internal enterprise workflow for sales and marketing teams. The talk covers architecture design, live deployment with demos, and production operations including failure modes and feedback loops. summary:
Dr. Sajjan Kanukolanu opens by stating that modern B2B buyers have largely made their decisions before contacting a vendor, citing Forrester 2026 research: 94% of buyers use GenAI as a primary research tool (a black box for sellers), 67% prefer a rep-free experience, 80% of deals go to buyers on the pre-contact list, and only 17% of total buying time is spent talking with vendors. He argues that most GTM teams fail by bolting AI onto existing stacks, which cannot identify buyers, capture intent signals, or evolve architecture. He frames three problems that must be solved together: (1) the AI problem—standalone AI cannot know the buyer; (2) the integration problem—old GTM stacks cannot capture intent signals and CRM context; (3) the architecture problem—AI must sit at the core.

He presents a three-layer architecture. The signals layer includes CRM data, visitor enrichment (de-anonymizing visitors), and social signals (especially LinkedIn engagement and job changes for tracking champions to new accounts). The buyer intelligence layer comprises a knowledge base (product, ICP, personas, playbooks), visitor identity, ICP scoring, buying-stage quantification, a context builder, and routing logic. Within this layer, an ICP filter agent weeds out contacts that don't fit criteria, a match agent checks contacts against the CRM for warmth, and an action agent decides next steps per person or buying committee—including Slack alerts with context, draft emails, and LinkedIn outreach. The action layer involves personalized chat, rep alerts, CRM updates with account context, and sequence triggers. A context graph connects all signals into a per-buyer record linking persona, account, and deal.

He then demos the Intelligence system: a personalized chat that references prior conversations instead of asking generic questions, an anonymous visitors dashboard showing ~3,000 visitors from ~280 accounts with industry breakdowns and hot signals, and a LinkedIn intelligence section tracking ~100 visitors from 73 companies engaging with eight posts, sortable by seniority.

He concludes with four failure modes: ICP drift (ICPs evolve but agents work off stale data without quarterly retraining on closed-won/lost deals), alert fatigue (flagging everything as hot destroys rep trust), identity ceiling (~70% company identification accuracy but only 15-20% individual identification—a structural limit), and human bottleneck (if editing an AI draft email takes longer than 30 seconds, reps will write their own). He leaves four takeaways: start with identity, separate fit and intent scoring, build an auditable and adjustable policy engine, and let the flywheel compound so every send, reply, and closed deal makes the model smarter.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: By the time a B2B buyer contacts a vendor, the decision is mostly made—only 17% of buying time is spent with vendors, and 80% of deals go to the pre-contact list.
Bolting AI onto existing GTM stacks fails because three problems—AI, integration, and architecture—must be solved simultaneously.
The three-layer architecture (signals, buyer intelligence, action) with a per-buyer context graph is the stable foundation; tools change but the architecture does not.
No single visitor-identification tool catches every visitor—multiple sources must be consolidated and deduped; identity accuracy is structurally limited (~70% company, 15-20% individual).
ICPs evolve over time; agents must be retrained quarterly with closed-won and closed-lost data or they will point to wrong accounts and people.
Alert fatigue kills system trust—use the knowledge base and context graph to surface only alerts that matter to sales reps.
If editing an AI-drafted email takes longer than 30 seconds, reps will abandon the system; shrink the friction to one-click approval.
Separate fit scoring from intent scoring—conflating them sends the wrong message to the wrong person.
Build an auditable, adjustable policy engine so GTM teams can diagnose and fix broken agent workflows without developer dependency.
Let the flywheel compound: every send, reply, and closed deal must feed back into the knowledge base to make the system smarter.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Sajjan introduces the premise that buyers are late-stage by the time they reach vendors and shares his background: 20+ years across product, technology, and marketing; VP of Global Operations and Strategy at Position²; leads AI-native transformation. He reports 75+ AI agents launched, 18+ vertical knowledge bases, 800+ runs per month as of June 2026.

sections.title: Three problems with bolting AI onto GTM stacks
sections.summary: Explains that bolting AI onto existing stacks hinders scale. Identifies three problems: (1) AI—standalone AI cannot know the buyer; (2) integration—old GTM stacks cannot capture intent signals and CRM context; (3) architecture—the underlying architecture must evolve with AI at the core. All three must be solved together.

sections.title: Buyer behavior statistics
sections.summary: Cites Forrester 2026 research: 94% of buyers use GenAI as primary research (a black box), 67% prefer rep-free experience, 80% of deals go to pre-contact list, only 17% of buying time is spent with vendors. Buyers have made up their minds before contacting the seller.

sections.title: Problem with generic AI chatbots
sections.summary: Describes how AI chatbots that ask 'How can I help you?' move the conversation backward because buyers have already done research. Sellers must know the buyer's identity and needs before the first message.

sections.title: Layer 1: Signals
sections.summary: Details the signals layer: CRM data (deals, contacts, owners), enrichment of anonymous visitors (accuracy is critical), and social signals—especially LinkedIn engagement and job changes. Explains how tracking a champion moving to a new account can automatically expand the account list.

sections.title: Layer 2: Buyer Intelligence
sections.summary: Describes buyer intelligence: knowledge base (product, ICP, personas, playbooks, success criteria), visitor identity, ICP scoring, buying-stage quantification, context builder, and routing logic determining channel, message, and timing for outreach.

sections.title: Layer 3: Action
sections.summary: Covers the action layer: personalized chat (addressing users by name, referencing prior visits, offering intent-based content), rep alerts (balanced quantity), CRM updates with account context, and sequence triggers for outreach timing.

sections.title: Context graph
sections.summary: Explains the context graph: a per-buyer connected record linking persona, account, and deal. Person signals link to accounts, accounts surface buying committees, and deal-level information tracks sales and marketing outreach, enabling prioritization of high-intent accounts.

sections.title: Implementation flow: identification and enrichment
sections.summary: Begins walking through the architecture as connected agents. When an anonymous visitor lands, the identification job uses multiple sources (no single tool catches every visitor), consolidates and dedupes, then sends data to the enrichment phase. Notes tools change but the architecture does not.

sections.title: ICP filter, match, and action agents
sections.summary: Details the buyer intelligence agents in action. The ICP filter agent checks contacts against knowledge base criteria (industry, geo, size, persona), deleting non-fits and moving qualified accounts into a clean table. The match agent checks contacts against CRM for warmth. The action agent decides next steps per person or buying committee—Slack alerts with context, draft emails, and LinkedIn outreach.

sections.title: Demo: Intelligence system personalized chat
sections.summary: Shows the Intelligence system's chat interface. Instead of generic greetings, it identifies the visitor on landing and references a prior conversation, offering to continue it with a clickable link. This reflects all collected signals and data personalized to the user.

sections.title: Demo: Anonymous visitors dashboard
sections.summary: Walks through the internal GTM dashboard's anonymous visitors section. The system identified ~3,000 visitors from ~280 accounts, with information technology as a key vertical. Shows industry breakdown, hot signals, contact details (company, location, industry), sortable by industry, seniority, and engagement. Names changed for privacy; titles accurate.

sections.title: Demo: LinkedIn intelligence dashboard
sections.summary: Shows the LinkedIn intelligence section—often missed by GTM teams. Over recent days, ~100 people from 73 companies visited via LinkedIn and engaged with eight posts. Contacts are sortable by C-suite, VPs, directors, managers, and ICs. Clicking into individuals reveals detailed engagement history, feeding intelligence back into the system.

sections.title: Failure mode 1: ICP drift
sections.summary: Explains that ICPs evolve over time. If a $20 AR company in one vertical closes but a $50-100 AR firm in a different vertical emerges as a new opportunity, the knowledge base must be updated. Without quarterly retraining on closed-won/lost deals, agents work off stale data and point to wrong accounts and people.

sections.title: Failure mode 2: Alert fatigue
sections.summary: If everything is flagged as hot, sales reps stop acting and stop trusting the system—it becomes dead. The knowledge base and context graph must cut through noise to surface only alerts from accounts and contacts that matter to sales.

sections.title: Failure mode 3: Identity ceiling
sections.summary: Describes a structural limit: visitor identification tools are ~70% accurate for company identification but only 15-20% for individual identification. The only mitigation is testing different systems for better numbers, but teams must keep these metrics in mind when planning GTM outreach.

sections.title: Failure mode 4: Human bottleneck
sections.summary: If the approval queue feels like a chore, it becomes backlogged and ignored. Draft emails should be nearly ready with minor edits, sendable with one click. If editing takes longer than 30 seconds, reps will write their own and the initiative is dead.

sections.title: Four key takeaways
sections.summary: Leaves four takeaways: (1) Start with identity—without visitor identification, GTM is dead; need a robust system with feedback loops to the knowledge base. (2) Separate score fit and intent—conflating them sends wrong messages. (3) Build an auditable, adjustable policy engine so GTM teams can diagnose and fix broken agent workflows without developers. (4) Let the flywheel compound—every send, reply, and closed deal must feed back into the knowledge base to make the model smarter.
